HCBPSYC314.topics: Developmental theories; Genetics and environment; Prenatal development and birth; Infancy and attachment; Cognitive and psychomotor development; Early and middle childhood; Play and education; Adolescence and psychopathology; Emerging and early adulthood; Middle and late adulthood; Relationships and personality development; Care and developmental interventions; Death, dying, grief and bereavement
HCBPSYC314.methods: Life-story interviewing; Theory-guided lifespan interview analysis; Developmental case-study analysis; Critical appraisal of developmental research and assessment reports

HCBPSYC315.name: Youth Resilience to Extremism
HCBPSYC315.contribution: Investigates psychosocial pathways into radicalisation, protective factors and interventions that support young people. It applies developmental and social psychology to resilience.
HCBPSYC315.topics: Radicalization, violent extremism and terrorism; Developmental and psychosocial pathways; Risk and protective factors; School climate and belonging; Identity and peer influence; Social-emotional learning and well-being; Empathy and perspective-taking; Conflict resolution and intercultural dialogue; Mental-health literacy and referral; Digital literacy and misinformation; Youth leadership and democratic participation; Counter- and alternative narratives
HCBPSYC315.methods: Primary-research synthesis; Intervention-evidence appraisal; Case and classroom-scenario analysis; Inclusive educational-resource design; Alternative-narrative development; Recipient-feedback collection and iterative revision; Ethical appraisal of prevention tools

MCCCOMM111.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
MCCCOMM111.contribution: studies rhetoric as it appears in political speech, social media and advertising and trains persuasive messages; it makes a specific complementary contribution to media and cultural studies through the analysis of public discourse
MCCCOMM111.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication
MCCCOMM111.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.contribution: studies persuasion, framing and nudging through communication studies, social psychology and neuroscience, including climate communication; it makes a specific complementary contribution to media and cultural studies at advanced level
MCCCOMM311.topics: Persuasion models and psychology; Ethics of persuasion; Coactive persuasion; Verbal and nonverbal communication; Message framing; Argumentation; Cognitive shortcuts and nudging; Science and sustainability communication; Circular lifestyles; Community-engaged communication
MCCCOMM311.methods: Persuasive-message design; Communication consulting and implementation; Literature review; Qualitative research diaries; Action research; Reflective case-study analysis; Gibbs reflective cycle

MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.contribution: gives a chronological overview of Western art history from the early Renaissance to the present; it directly implements the arts direction
MCCHEAM111.topics: Late-medieval and Renaissance art; Mannerism; Baroque and Rococo; Enlightenment and Romanticism; Realism and Impressionism; Post-Impressionism, Symbolism and Art Nouveau; Modernism and Cubism; Interwar art; Postwar and postmodern art; Contemporary art; Artistic form and historical context
MCCHEAM111.methods: Close visual analysis of paintings; Composition, space, form, tone and colour analysis; On-site artwork study; Historical contextualization; Art-historical text analysis

MCCHEAM112.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
MCCHEAM112.contribution: examines how making objects shapes human societies and identities from early settlements to classical antiquity; it directly implements the cultural studies direction through material culture
MCCHEAM112.topics: Materiality, craft and cognition; Settlement and landscape; Neolithic and Bronze Age communities; Craft production and social hierarchy; Trade and exchange; Pottery and iconography; Seals, textiles and elite identities; Domestic and urban craft spaces; Archaeological interpretation; Ancient technology and community identity; Contemporary archaeology
MCCHEAM112.methods: Artefact observation, measurement and cataloguing; Archaeological technical drawing; Visual and stylistic analysis; Comparative material-culture analysis; Archaeological database and literature research; Material-evidence-based argumentation; Archaeological educational-game design; Contemporary archaeological data collection and hypothesis development

MCCHEAM312.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
MCCHEAM312.contribution: examines debates on modern art and how museums and exhibitions shape public perception; it directly implements advanced arts and cultural studies
MCCHEAM312.topics: Modernism and avant-gardes; Cubism and abstraction; Modern architecture and design; Figuration and Mexican muralism; Abstract Expressionism; Minimalism and Pop Art; Postmodernism and conceptual art; Photography, installation, performance and video art; Globalization and contemporary art; Authorship, originality and medium; Museums, curating and reception; Eurocentrism in art history
MCCHEAM312.methods: Art-historical interpretation and contextual analysis; Critical analysis of museums and curatorial practices; Scholarly literature review; Independent art-historical research

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.contribution: Develops art-historical research, visual analysis and academic writing in the arts and culture sequence.
MCCHEAM316.topics: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
MCCLITR111.contribution: introduces the interpretation of literary forms including novels, graphic narratives and film narration; it directly implements the arts and literature direction
MCCLITR111.topics: Definitions and value of literature; Literary genre and originality; Story, plot and narrative structure; Character, setting and point of view; Symbolism and allegory; Style, tone, humour and irony; Graphic fiction and microfiction; Creative nonfiction and memoir; Children's literature; Poetic language, imagery, sound and form; Drama and tragedy; Film adaptation
MCCLITR111.methods: Close reading; Formalist literary analysis; Narrative analysis; Poetic and dramatic analysis; Critical-source integration; Literary essay and review construction

MCCLITR112.name: Great Literary Works
MCCLITR112.contribution: gives a chronological overview of major literary texts from the Epic of Gilgamesh to postmodernity and their themes; it directly implements the arts and literature direction
MCCLITR112.topics: Literature, canon and world literature; Epic and heroism; Tragedy, fate and identity; Autobiography and memory; Framed storytelling and narrative power; Gender and agency; Essay and philosophical tale; Satire and irony; Colonialism and its critique; Modernist narration and subjectivity; Alienation and family; Art, sexuality and civilization; Magical realism
MCCLITR112.methods: Close literary reading; Formalist analysis of genre, theme and technique; Comparative textual interpretation; Narrative analysis; Critical-source interpretation and integration

MCCLITR211.name: World Myth & Literature
MCCLITR211.contribution: compares ancient and world myths and literary traditions across cultures; it directly implements the arts and literature and cultural studies directions
MCCLITR211.topics: Creation and divine succession myths; Myth and cultural power; Gender and exchange; Epic and tragedy; Women, war and narrative agency; Focalization; Hero structures and motifemes; Cross-cultural storytelling; Myth in text, image and performance; Reception and adaptation; Ovid's Metamorphoses
MCCLITR211.methods: Comparative myth analysis; Structuralist narrative analysis and Propp's motifemes; Focalization analysis; Gender-focused literary analysis; Primary-source and scholarly-literature research; Cross-cultural narrative adaptation

MCCLITR212.name: Life & Travel Writing
MCCLITR212.contribution: analyses memoir, autobiography, travel writing and blogs and develops writing and debating skills; it directly implements the arts and literature direction
MCCLITR212.topics: Autobiography and memoir culture; Fact, fiction and autobiographical truth; Autobiographical pact; Self and multiple identities; Individual and collective memory; Experience, embodiment and agency; Ethics and traumatic memory; Grief and disability narratives; Popular memoir and narrative technique; Digital self-presentation; Travel and spiritual self-fashioning; Migration, language and cultural identity
MCCLITR212.methods: Close life-narrative analysis; Smith and Watson's strategies for reading life narratives; Theory-guided analysis of memory, identity, embodiment and agency; Comparative textual and contextual interpretation; Structured autobiographical creative writing

MCCLITR311.name: Film & Text
MCCLITR311.contribution: analyses film adaptations of literary texts with interpretive strategies and cultural analysis; it directly implements advanced arts, literature and media studies
MCCLITR311.topics: Literature-film relationships; Narrative and medium specificity; Fidelity debates; Cinematography and mise-en-scène; Editing, continuity and montage; Film music and sound; Intertextuality; Auteurism; Adaptation and heritage; Adaptation markets; Spectatorship and immersion
MCCLITR311.methods: Formalist literary analysis; Close film-sequence analysis; Comparative text-film analysis; Intertextual analysis; Theory-led adaptation research

MCCLITR312.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
MCCLITR312.contribution: examines how humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural-minority and psychoanalytic perspectives affect interpretation and has students carry out a research project on selected texts; it directly implements advanced literary research
MCCLITR312.topics: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.

MCCMEDI111.name: Introduction to Film & Media
MCCMEDI111.contribution: introduces the history of cinema and how films work as an evolving cultural form; it directly implements the media studies direction

MCCMEDI111.methods: Close film and media analysis; Historical and cultural contextualization; Application of feminist and postcolonial film theory; Independent analytical or creative-analytical media research

MCCMEDI112.name: Media Archaeology
MCCMEDI112.contribution: examines pre-digital media technologies such as typewriters, cassette tapes and early printed books and how they shaped knowledge; it directly implements the media studies direction through material and historical analysis
MCCMEDI112.topics: Media materiality and memory; Print culture; Optics and projection; Telegraphy and infrastructure; Mechanical inscription; Broadcasting and sound fidelity; Portable analogue media; Cassette revival; Computing and networks; Media geology; Technological obsolescence; Mechanical reproduction and aura
MCCMEDI112.methods: Media-archaeological artifact analysis; Historical and technical media comparison; Facsimile and manuscript-print analysis; Media-protocol investigation; Comparative listening and sound-fidelity analysis; Analogue recording exercises; Historical media-object research

MCCMEDI211.name: From T.V. to TikTok

MCCMEDI312.contribution: traces the development of the documentary form and has students produce a short documentary, analysing non-fiction representations in their historical and social contexts; it makes a specific complementary contribution through media studies and the research-based documentary project UCM offers
MCCMEDI312.topics: Documentary definition, modes and ethics; Early documentary and city symphonies; Soviet filmmaking; European documentary traditions; Direct cinema and cinéma vérité; Audio and public-affairs documentary; Propaganda and advocacy; Historical and ethnographic documentary; Nature documentary; Mockumentary; Interactive and autobiographical documentary; Documentary aesthetics

candidateDecisions.label: Psychology, cognitive science and neuroscience, biomedical science and global health (sciences domain)
Arts and literature, cultural studies and media studies (humanities domain)
Business administration, economics and international development (social-science domain)
Information and computer science and mathematics (science domain)

analysis: Politics and society builds from philosophy, modern history, comparative institutions, law and sociology to EU governance, conflict, advanced social theory and historical research. Climate and governance give cross-domain breadth, while data, statistics and qualitative inquiry contribute different methods. This supports the strongest shared-core comparison without claiming a formal concentration replica or laboratory research. Mind and health owns the natural-science research direction through gateways, physiology, molecular biology, lab practice, neuroscience, pathology and evidence synthesis. Psycholinguistics was available only in the first spring, ahead of appropriate cognitive-science depth. Life Science Laboratory in the fourth term supplies substantive experimental work after the life-science gateway and earlier molecular biology, with developmental psychology moving to the final spring after psychopathology. The literature and media direction develops interpretation of literature, cinema, material culture, public rhetoric and visual art into advanced research, communication and documentary production. The UCM catalogue shows distinct concentration directions in economics and development and computing and mathematics. These coherent candidates remain outside the three-option limit. Shared academic methods and thematic breadth do not erase the separation of 22, 19 and 23 courses each way. Aligned rows capture specific overlapping learning and the unmatched fixed requirements show the limits of comparison.

alignment.rationale: Both study modern world history, including twentieth-century conflicts and political change. UCR surveys a longer period beginning in the nineteenth century.
Both study political thought and apply arguments about society and political authority to contemporary questions.
UCR’s introductory philosophy course explores knowledge and argument. Maastricht has a dedicated course on how scientific knowledge is produced and justified.
Both develop academic writing, argument and reflection on learning. The UCR course also covers personal and professional development.
Maastricht dedicates a core course to the purposes and practice of liberal arts and sciences education.
Both introduce research questions and study design. UCR adds statistical analysis, while Maastricht introduces qualitative and quantitative approaches.
Both develop qualitative research design and data collection. Maastricht uses this training to prepare a proposal for its linked Research Project.
Maastricht requires a separate project that develops academic inquiry and writing.
Maastricht requires a standalone first-year project following its two introductory methods trainings. UCR includes research projects within individual courses.
Maastricht requires a set of dedicated skills trainings. UCR develops methods through courses such as Qualitative Research Methodology and Statistics & Experimental Methods.
Maastricht requires three concentration projects. UCR develops related skills through documentary production and historical research courses.
This example uses three courses (15 EC) across the two domains outside a single concentration. The approved two-domain route instead requires one or two courses in the third domain.
This example uses fifteen courses (75 EC) in one domain. Concentration study combines introductory, intermediate and advanced work, including at least 20 EC of advanced coursework.
Maastricht requires a 20 EC Capstone. The 15 EC independent research option shown for UCR is separate from the scheduled courses.
